[QUERENT] "the grammar of incarnation"

[ANSWER]

The grammar of incarnation refers to the structural logic, language, and theological rules through which the abstract or divine ("the Word" or Logos) translates into material, flesh, or text. [1, 2, 3]
Key Dimensions of the Concept

* Mediation of the Divine: In Christian theology, the grammar of incarnation asserts that physical, particular, and material reality can genuinely bear and mediate the presence of God. As theologian Donald MacKinnon and others have explored, it governs how divine-human identity and kenosis (self-emptying) are articulated without reducing the divine to the human or vice versa. [1, 2]
* Word Made Flesh vs. Word Made Text: In biblical and literary studies (such as analyses of the Gospel of John and the prologue), the concept examines how speech transitions into durable writing or bodily form, linking communicative syntax with physical presence. [1, 2, 3]
* Resurrection and Embodiment: The grammar of incarnation establishes that embodiment and corporeality are inherently capax divinitatis (capable of containing or expressing the divine), making subsequent theological structures like the Resurrection an intensification of physical presence rather than an escape from it. [1]

For further readings and specific reflections on how this phrase is used in theological and literary contexts, you can explore discussions like The Word Became Flesh: John and the Grammar of Incarnation or community resources like The Grammar of Incarnation - St. Philips Episcopal Church. [1, 2]
